title: Kedoshim: no stumbling block (Leviticus 19:14)
hookLine: don't put a stumbling block before the blind; the rabbis read it as never misleading anyone

lines: A FRIEND ASKS ABOUT A CAR.
A BLIND MAN AND A ROAD.
cards: A friend is about to buy a used car, and asks what you think. You happen to know the transmission is shot. You also happen to want that car yourself, and if they pass, the price will drop.
So you say, eh, I'd look at other options. Nobody would ever know why you said it. Nothing you said was even false.
Leviticus 19 has a short verse about a blind man and an obstacle in the road. The rabbis read it, and found your friend and the car inside it.

teach.h: DON'T TRIP THE ONE WHO CAN'T SEE.
teach.b: The verse, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "Thou shalt not curse the deaf, nor put a stumbling-block before the blind, but thou shalt fear thy God: I am the LORD." Plainly, it means what it says.
Don't trip someone who can't see it coming. Don't curse someone who can't hear it. Then the widening.

The Sifra, an early rabbinic commentary on Leviticus, reads the blind as anyone blind in a matter, anyone who can't see what you can see. If someone asks your advice, don't give advice that isn't good for them.
Its example: don't say sell your field and buy a donkey, when you're secretly planning to buy that field yourself.

teach.h: NO CUP FOR THE ONE WHO VOWED.
teach.b: The Talmud stretches it further: don't hand a cup of wine to someone who has vowed not to drink. Don't help another person do the wrong they're already reaching for.
A stumbling block can be an offer, a nudge, a door held open. And why does the verse close with fear thy God? Rashi answers: because nobody else can check.
Only you know whether your advice was honest or self-serving.
That's exactly what makes the other person blind in this matter, and why the verse hands the case to God.
Today the principle is cited in Jewish discussions of business ethics, financial advice and selling to people who can't judge what they're buying.

how: Jewish law applies lifnei iver, the stumbling-block principle, to advice, business dealings and helping others do wrong, and it appears in rabbinic rulings on everything from selling dangerous goods to giving biased counsel.

o: a stumbling block put before the blind
the curse laid on someone who can't hear
holy ones: the portion of Leviticus 19

games.q: what's inside the verse — tap the pairs.
p: sell your field, buy a donkey
not for one who vowed off it

s: the rabbis read this verse only about physical obstacles
the Sifra widens it to anyone blind in a matter, including bad advice.
Rashi says the verse ends with fear of God because no one else can check your intent
only you know whether your advice was honest.
helping someone do a wrong they want to do is fine under this verse
the Talmud counts handing wine to someone who vowed off it as a stumbling block.

games.q: a neighbor asks if they should sell their field and buy a donkey. you'd love to buy that field. what does the Sifra say?
o: give them the advice that's good for them.
games.why: the Sifra uses this very case: don't give advice that isn't good for them. that's a stumbling block before the blind.

practice: Think of someone who has asked your opinion lately, or is about to: about a job, a purchase, a relationship. Ask yourself honestly whether you'd gain anything from what you tell them, or are tempted to leave something out.
Then picture giving the advice you'd want in their place, even if it costs you something.

wordCard.voice: Kedoshim. The portion that forbids a stumbling block before the blind, which the rabbis read as never misleading anyone who can't see what you see.

orig.note: Hebrew: "before the blind": the name the rabbis give the stumbling-block principle.

carryVoice: Your line: no stumbling blocks. Only you can see behind your own advice. Day four hundred twelve, done.

sources.q: Thou shalt not curse the deaf, nor put a stumbling-block before the blind, but thou shalt fear thy God: I am the LORD.
